headline: Washington Tribe Poised to Reclaim 1,100 Ancestral Acres After Century Underwater
meta_description: The Lower Elwha Klallam tribe awaits a presidential signature to recover 1,100 acres of ancestral land along the Elwha River, flooded for over a century by a n…
summary_short: After 171 years, the Lower Elwha Klallam tribe is one signature away from reclaiming 1,100 ancestral acres along Washington's Elwha River, restoring both land and salmon…
body:
A century of waiting may finally end for the Lower Elwha Klallam tribe. A federal bill already passed by both houses of Congress now awaits only a presidential signature to return 1,100 acres of ancestral land along the Elwha River—territory that has been underwater or inaccessible for 171 years. The parcel, located between state highways 101 and 112, includes sacred sites where tribal elders say their people were blessed into existence by the Creator, as well as historic villages integral to Klallam identity. The land transfer would effectively reverse the 1855 Point No Point Treaty, which had ceded most of the tribe's territory in exchange for education, healthcare, and hunting and fishing rights—promises complicated by the 1910 construction of the Elwha Dam, which flooded these very acres and severed the Klallams' ancestral way of life for generations.

The recovery of this land carries deeper meaning than acreage alone. Tribal Chair Melissa Gilman articulated what most government documents miss: "Our land isn't just land. The river isn't just the river. The salmon aren't just salmon. This is part of who we are as people." For over a century, chinook salmon and trout lost access to crucial spawning grounds upstream. Since the dam's demolition two decades ago, the ecosystem has begun to heal—and remarkably, 2026 marks the fourth consecutive year tribal members have successfully exercised their fishing rights along the river.

The precedent is encouraging. When dams were removed from the nearby Klamath River, salmon reappeared in the upper reaches within a single year. As the Elwha continues its own restoration, the Klallam people stand ready to reclaim not just land, but the relationship with river and salmon that defines them. Vanessa Castle, a tribe member, captured the moment's significance: "That last missing piece was the Klallams, the people of the land. And now that can happen in a way that feels fulfilling and respectful, and that we have a space that we can call home again."
quick_facts: 1,100 acres of Klallam ancestral land awaiting presidential signature for return
Located along Elwha River between State Highway 101 and Route 112
Land flooded since 1910 dam construction, underwater for over 114 years
Fourth consecutive year (2026) tribal members exercising fishing rights
Lower Elwha Klallam tribe regaining territory 171 years after losing it
